title: Falling: why a falling thing speeds up, and why it stops speeding up

summary.text: A raindrop falls from a cloud two kilometres up and only taps your head. A stone dropped from a first-floor balcony would sting your toe. Your child finds out why, by dropping paper cupcake liners, a ball of dough while walking, and a marble into soft dough from three heights. They learn that a falling thing gains the same speed every second, until the push of the air matches the pull of the Earth. They see that sideways speed and falling do not disturb each other, why a mouse can fall safely and a horse cannot, and how Galileo's first idea about falling turned out to be wrong.
summary.art: A raindrop high in a grey cloud and a small stone on a balcony rail, with a child's open hand below catching one raindrop on the palm.

intro.hook: A raindrop falls from a cloud about 2 kilometres up. A pebble dropped from a first-floor balcony, only 3 metres up, would sting your toe. How can a raindrop that falls so much farther be so gentle?
intro.text: If nothing slowed it, the raindrop would hit the ground at about 700 kilometres an hour. That is almost as fast as an aeroplane. But something does slow it. In this unit you find out what, by dropping paper cupcake liners and a ball of dough. You will also find out why a ball that you drop while walking does not land at your feet.
intro.art: A raindrop drawn at three heights in the sky, small speed arrows beside it, and a pebble on a balcony rail above a child's bare foot.

outcomes: I can say that a falling thing gains the same extra speed every second, about 10 metres a second more, and use this to find its speed after 1, 2 and 3 seconds.
I can explain why a falling thing in air stops speeding up: the push of the air grows with speed until it equals the pull of gravity. I can name this top speed.
I can run a fair test that shows a heavier thing of the same shape reaches a higher top speed, and explain why.
I can show that sideways speed and falling are separate, and explain why a ball tossed up in a moving train comes back to my hand.
I can show that a thing falling twice as fast makes a dent four times as deep, and say that movement energy grows with speed times speed.
I can explain why a mouse can survive a fall that would break a horse, using weight and the area the air pushes on.
I can tell how Galileo's first idea about falling was wrong and how it was shown wrong. I can name something about falling that nobody can yet predict.

terms.meaning: How far something moves in a certain time, such as in one second or one hour.
terms.example: A child walking at an easy pace moves about 1 metre every second.
terms.art: A child walking across a room with a number 1 metre per second above her head.

terms.meaning: How fast the speed of something is changing. Speeding up is a kind of acceleration.
terms.example: A falling stone gains about 10 metres a second of speed every second.
terms.art: A falling stone drawn three times, with speed numbers 10, 20 and 30 beside it.

terms.meaning: The push of the air against anything that moves through it. It gets bigger as the thing goes faster.
terms.example: You feel air resistance as a strong push on your hand when you hold it out of a moving bus.
terms.art: A hand held out flat from a bus window with small arrows of air pushing back against it.

terms.meaning: The top speed of a falling thing in air. At this speed the push of the air up equals the pull of gravity down, so the thing stops speeding up.
terms.example: A big raindrop has a terminal speed of about 30 kilometres an hour.
terms.art: A raindrop with a long down arrow for the pull and an equal up arrow for the push of the air.

terms.meaning: How fast a thing moves along, not up or down.
terms.example: A bus moving along the road has sideways speed, and so do the people inside it.
terms.art: A bus on a coastal road with a straight arrow pointing forward along the road.

terms.meaning: The way a thing keeps moving as it is moving, or keeps still, unless something pushes or pulls it.
terms.example: You lurch forward when a bus brakes, because your body keeps moving forward.
terms.art: Passengers in a bus all leaning forward as the bus brakes.

terms.meaning: The line a thing follows as it moves through the air. The path of a thrown ball is a curve called a parabola.
terms.example: A ball thrown to a friend follows a curved path, up and then down.
terms.art: A ball thrown between two children, with a dotted curved line showing its path.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is moving. It grows with speed times speed. Scientists also call it kinetic energy.
terms.example: A cricket ball at twice the speed has four times the movement energy, so it can dig a much deeper dent.
terms.art: Two cricket balls hitting soft dough, a slow one making a small dent and a fast one making a deep dent.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is held high up. It turns into movement energy as the thing falls.
terms.example: A coconut high in a palm has stored energy. When it falls, this becomes movement energy.
terms.art: A coconut hanging high in a palm tree and the same coconut halfway down, with a label of stored energy and movement energy.

terms.meaning: The amount of outside that a thing has. The air can only push on the outside.
terms.example: A wide umbrella has a bigger surface area than a closed one, so the air pushes on it more.
terms.art: An open umbrella and a closed umbrella side by side, with the outside of the open one shaded.

terms.meaning: A number multiplied by itself. The square of 3 is 3 times 3, which is 9.
terms.example: Twice the speed gives 2 times 2, which is 4 times the movement energy.
terms.art: A grid of 3 rows and 3 columns of dots with the sum 3 times 3 equals 9 beside it.

explanations.concept: A falling thing gains the same speed every second
explanations.definition: Without air, a falling thing gains about 10 metres a second of speed every second. The steady pull of the Earth gives a steady speeding up.
explanations.description: Drop a ball. At the start its speed is zero. After 1 second it moves at about 10 metres a second. After 2 seconds it moves at about 20. After 3 seconds it moves at about 30. Each second adds the same 10. The Earth pulls the ball with the same pull all the way down, and a steady pull adds speed at a steady rate. The exact number is 9.8 metres a second every second, and we round it to 10 to make the sums easy. A speed of 10 metres a second is 36 kilometres an hour. So after 3 seconds the ball is going 108 kilometres an hour. How far the ball has fallen grows even faster. It is about 5 metres after 1 second, 20 metres after 2 seconds and 45 metres after 3 seconds.
examples: A coconut that falls for 1 second hits the ground at about 36 kilometres an hour, if the air is not in the way.
A cliff diver who falls for 2 seconds is going about 72 kilometres an hour when she hits the water.
A dough ball dropped from table height, 1 metre, is moving at about 16 kilometres an hour when it lands.
explanations.art: A ball falling beside a tall wall marked in metres, drawn at 1, 2 and 3 seconds, with the speeds 10, 20 and 30 metres a second written beside it.
explanations.context: How fast is a falling thing going after one second, two seconds or three? This card gives the rule and the numbers.

chart.title: Speed of a falling stone, second by second (without air)
chart.note: These are rounded numbers. In real air, a stone dropped from a high place stops speeding up before it lands.

explanations.concept: Terminal speed: the air pushes back harder the faster you fall
explanations.definition: Terminal speed is the top speed of a falling thing in air. It is the speed at which the push of the air up equals the pull of gravity down.
explanations.description: A falling thing has to push the air out of its way. The faster it goes, the more air particles it hits each second, and the harder it hits them. So the push of the air grows as the speed grows. A rough rule is that twice the speed gives four times the push. At the start the push of the air is tiny, and the pull of gravity wins, so the thing speeds up. At some speed the push of the air grows as big as the pull. The two are now equal, so nothing is left to speed the thing up. It falls at a steady speed. Gravity has not stopped pulling. The air is pushing back just as hard.
examples: A big raindrop reaches about 30 kilometres an hour within a few metres of falling, and then falls at that steady speed all the way down.
A skydiver lying flat falls at about 200 kilometres an hour. If she pulls in her arms and legs and dives head first, she meets less air and falls faster, at about 250 to 290.
A peregrine falcon that folds her wings and dives passes 200 kilometres an hour.
explanations.art: A skydiver lying flat with a long arrow down for her weight, an equal arrow up for the push of the air, and the words steady speed beside her.
explanations.context: Why does a raindrop not hit like a bullet? This card explains how the air sets a top speed for anything that falls.

explanations.concept: A heavier thing of the same shape has a higher top speed
explanations.definition: If two things have the same shape and size, the heavier one has the higher terminal speed. Four times the weight gives about twice the terminal speed.
explanations.description: In a vacuum, heavy and light things fall together. In air, the shape and size also matter. Take two things of the same shape. The heavier one is pulled harder by the Earth. So the air has to push harder before the two forces are equal. The air pushes harder only when the thing goes faster. So the heavier thing must go faster before it stops speeding up. Because the push of the air grows as speed times speed, four times the push needs only twice the speed. That is why a stack of four cupcake liners falls much faster than one liner, but not four times faster.
examples: A solid rubber ball and a hollow plastic ball are the same size. In air the rubber ball falls faster, because it is heavier.
A stack of four cupcake liners reaches the floor before one cupcake liner.
A big hailstone falls faster than a small one, because it has more weight for the same shape.
explanations.art: One paper cup and a stack of four paper cups falling side by side, with the stack ahead of the single cup.
explanations.context: In the Drop Race you saw that heavy and light things land together without air. This card explains why the air changes the answer.

explanations.concept: Sideways speed and falling are separate
explanations.definition: A thing that moves sideways and falls does both at once. Gravity changes only the falling part. The sideways speed stays the same unless the air or something else pushes on it.
explanations.description: Drop a ball while you walk. It does not fall straight down to the floor beneath your hand. It keeps moving forward at your walking speed while it falls. So it lands ahead of the spot where you let go. How far ahead? The time it takes to fall, times your walking speed. A fall from the height of your shoulder takes about half a second. At a walking speed of 1 metre a second, the ball lands about half a metre ahead. A ball rolled off a table and a ball dropped from the same height land at the same moment, because gravity pulls both of them down in the same way. Galileo showed in 1638 that the path of a thrown thing is a curve, and the curve is a sideways movement and a falling movement added together.
examples: A ball rolled off a table and a ball dropped from the table's edge land at the same moment.
A cricket ball hit for a six rises and falls along a curve. The falling part follows the same rule as a dropped ball.
Water from a tap that points sideways falls in a curve. Water that runs faster lands farther away, but it takes the same time to fall.
explanations.art: A girl walking along a line of tape and letting go of a ball, with dots showing the ball landing ahead of the spot below her hand.
explanations.context: Where does a ball land when you let go of it while walking? This card explains why it lands ahead of your hand.

explanations.concept: Why a ball tossed up in a moving train comes back to your hand
explanations.definition: A thing tossed up inside a smoothly moving train already shares the train's sideways speed. It keeps that speed while it rises and falls, so it comes back to your hand.
explanations.description: A ball tossed up in a train that moves at 80 kilometres an hour is also moving forward at 80 kilometres an hour. Gravity does not take that sideways speed away. The air in the carriage moves with the train too. So while the ball is up, it moves forward exactly as far as you do, and it drops back into your hand. This means that you cannot tell from this test whether the train is moving. Galileo wrote about this in 1632. He said that nothing you do below decks in a smoothly moving ship shows whether the ship is moving. The Earth is a very big ship. It turns once a day and travels around the Sun. You and everything near you share its sideways speed, and so a coconut falls to the foot of the palm and not far to the west.
examples: A pen tossed up in a smoothly moving bus lands back in your hand.
A coconut falls straight down beside the palm even though the Earth turns at hundreds of metres a second beneath it.
A cup of tea on a train table stays where it is, until the train brakes or turns.
explanations.art: A girl on a train seat tossing a lime straight up, with a dotted line showing the lime moving forward with the train and landing in her hand.
explanations.context: A ball tossed up in a moving train comes back to your hand. This card explains why, and what it tells us about the Earth.

explanations.concept: The old argument about a turning Earth
explanations.description: In 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote in his book the Aryabhatiya that the Earth turns once a day, and that the stars only seem to move west. He gave a picture: a person in a boat moving forward sees still things on the bank slide backward. Later astronomers disagreed. As the argument is usually told, Varahamihira said that if the Earth turned, birds that left their nests could not find them again, and Brahmagupta is reported to have said the same of things thrown into the air. This was a sensible argument. What they did not have was the idea that a thing in the air keeps the sideways speed it had. Galileo gave this idea in the 1600s. A ball tossed up in a moving train shows it. Today nobody doubts that the Earth turns.
examples: A bird that leaves a nest in a tree on the turning Earth still shares the Earth's sideways speed, so she can fly back to the same tree.
A stone thrown straight up on the turning Earth lands back in your hand.

perspectives.explanation: The Earth turns, and the stars only seem to move. He compared it to a person in a moving boat who sees things on the bank move backward.

perspectives.who: Varahamihira and Brahmagupta, about 505 CE and 628 CE
perspectives.explanation: The Earth cannot be turning. If it were, a stone thrown up or a bird that left her nest would be left behind. They had no idea yet that a thing in the air keeps its sideways speed.

explanations.art: Two astronomers on a stone terrace arguing, one pointing at a boat moving across a river and the other pointing at a bird leaving a nest.
explanations.context: Long before trains, Indian astronomers argued about whether the Earth turns. This card explains the argument and what was missing from it.

explanations.concept: Movement energy: twice the speed, four times the dent
explanations.definition: The movement energy of a thing grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed gives four times the movement energy, and three times the speed gives nine times.
explanations.description: A ball held high has stored energy. As it falls, the stored energy turns into movement energy. When the ball hits something soft, the movement energy goes into making a dent. A little of it also becomes sound and a tiny bit of heat. If you drop a ball from 4 times the height, it hits with twice the speed, when the air is not in the way. In the 1720s, a Dutch scientist named Willem 's Gravesande dropped brass balls into soft clay. A ball with twice the speed dug a dent about 4 times as deep. A French scientist named Emilie du Chatelet used his results in her book of 1740 to argue that the strength of a moving thing depends on speed times speed, and not on speed alone. This is also why a car going twice as fast needs about four times the distance to stop.
examples: A car going 60 kilometres an hour needs about 4 times the distance to stop of a car going 30 kilometres an hour.
A marble dropped from 40 centimetres lands with twice the speed of a marble dropped from 10 centimetres.
Water at the bottom of a high waterfall hits the pool far harder than water from a low step.
explanations.art: A marble above a slab of soft dough at three heights, with a small, a medium and a deep dent beneath, and the speeds 1, 1.4 and 2 beside them.
explanations.context: Why does a fall from higher up hurt so much more? This card explains how speed and the strength of a hit are linked.

explanations.concept: Why a mouse can fall and a horse cannot
explanations.definition: When an animal gets bigger, her weight grows faster than the area of her body that the air pushes on. So a bigger animal has a higher terminal speed and hits the ground harder.
explanations.description: Take a cube that is 1 centimetre wide. Now make a cube that is twice as wide, 2 centimetres. It weighs 8 times as much, because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. But its outside is only 4 times as big, because 2 times 2 is 4. The air can only push on the outside. So the bigger cube has more weight for each bit of outside. It must fall faster before the air pushes back enough. Animals work the same way. In 1926, the scientist J. B. S. Haldane wrote that a mouse dropped down a deep mine shaft gets only a slight shock and walks away, while a rat is killed, a man is broken and a horse splashes. A small animal has little weight for her size, and an ant is hardly hurt by any fall.
examples: An ant dropped from a roof walks away, because her top speed is low.
The winged seeds of the sal tree spin down slowly, because they have a large wing for a tiny weight.
A flying squirrel spreads out skin flaps to make a bigger area, so the air pushes on her more.
explanations.art: A mouse, a cat and a horse falling beside a tall wall, with a tiny puff at the mouse's landing and a large crash at the horse's landing.
explanations.context: Small animals survive falls that would break big ones. This card explains why, using what you found about weight and air.

explanations.concept: Falling stars: a fall from space
explanations.definition: A meteor is a speck of rock or metal from space that falls into the Earth's air so fast that the air in front of it glows. The bright streak is called a shooting star.
explanations.description: Most meteors are no bigger than a grain of sand or a small pebble. They hit the Earth's air at between 11 and 72 kilometres every second. At that speed the air cannot get out of the way. It is squeezed in front of the speck and gets very hot, and the heat makes the speck glow and boil away. Most meteors glow about 80 to 100 kilometres above the ground, and nothing reaches the ground. A larger piece that does survive, called a meteorite, is slowed by the air to its terminal speed in the last few kilometres. By then it is falling like a stone from a tall building, not like a shooting star.
examples: The Perseid meteors that you can see each August are tiny specks left by a comet.
A meteorite that lands is often cool to touch, because it has fallen slowly for the last part of its journey.
explanations.art: A night sky over a Chennai rooftop with a bright shooting star streak and a faint glowing trail of squeezed hot air behind it.
explanations.context: A shooting star is a fall from space. This card explains why it glows, using the push of the air.

explanations.definition: The Moon, Mars and Jupiter pull things down by different amounts, so a falling thing gains speed at a different rate on each.
explanations.description: On Earth, a falling thing gains about 10 metres a second of speed every second. On the Moon it gains only about 1.6 metres a second every second, six times less, because the Moon is smaller and pulls less. On Mars it gains about 3.7. On Jupiter, at the top of the clouds, it gains about 25. A ball dropped from the height of a table, 1 metre, takes about 0.45 seconds to land on Earth. It takes 1.1 seconds on the Moon, 0.7 seconds on Mars and 0.3 seconds on Jupiter. The rule stays the same on every world. The speed grows by the same amount each second. Only the size of the amount changes.
examples: The astronauts who jumped on the Moon seemed to fall in slow motion, because they gained speed six times more slowly.
A ball dropped on Mars takes about 1.6 times as long to land as on Earth.
explanations.art: Four balls dropped from the same height on the Moon, Mars, Earth and Jupiter, each with a clock showing how long it takes to land.
explanations.context: Does a ball fall the same way on the Moon? This card compares falling on four worlds.

chart.title: How much speed a falling thing gains each second
chart.note: Rounded numbers. For Jupiter, the number is at the top of the clouds.

agreed.text: Without air, everything near the Earth gains the same speed each second, about 9.8 metres a second.
agreed.evidence: The Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott let a hammer and a feather fall on the Moon in 1971, and they landed together. In 2022, a French satellite named MICROSCOPE showed that two different metals fall alike, to about 1 part in 10 to the power of 15.

agreed.text: In air, a falling thing reaches a top speed when the push of the air equals its weight.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured the speeds of falling water drops of different sizes in still air in 1949, and found that each size reaches a steady speed. Skydivers' recorded speeds show the same thing.

agreed.text: A thing that moves sideways and falls does both at once, and the path is a curve.
agreed.evidence: Galileo described this in 1638. Photographs of two balls, one dropped and one thrown sideways at the same moment, show them at the same height at every flash.

agreed.text: Movement energy grows with speed times speed.
agreed.evidence: 's Gravesande's clay-dent tests in the 1720s, and modern measurements of car stopping distances, both show that twice the speed gives four times the effect.

agreed.text: Bigger animals reach higher terminal speeds than smaller ones, so they are hurt more by a fall.
agreed.evidence: Weight grows with the cube of an animal's length and area grows with the square, so the air pushes on a big animal less for her weight. J. B. S. Haldane described this in 1926.

challenging.claim: A falling thing keeps speeding up until it lands.
challenging.who: Many people, and many textbook pictures that leave out the air.
challenging.for: For short falls, such as a dropped pen, the air hardly matters, and the thing really does speed up all the way. On the Moon, with no air, it is true for every fall.
challenging.against: A raindrop from a high cloud and a skydiver both stop speeding up. The push of the air grows until it equals the pull of the Earth.

challenging.claim: A coin dropped from a skyscraper could kill a person on the ground.
challenging.who: A story many people have heard.
challenging.for: A coin has fallen a very long way, so it seems it should be going extremely fast.
challenging.against: A coin tumbles in the air and reaches a terminal speed of only about 50 to 80 kilometres an hour. It can sting, but it does not have enough movement energy to be deadly.

challenging.claim: A ball thrown hard sideways stays in the air longer than a ball that is dropped.
challenging.who: A common idea, because the thrown ball travels farther.
challenging.for: A thrown ball goes a long way, so it seems that it must stay up for a long time.
challenging.against: Gravity pulls down the same way on both balls. A ball rolled off a table and a ball dropped from its edge land at the same moment.

challenging.claim: The speed of a falling thing grows in proportion to the distance it has fallen.
challenging.who: Galileo Galilei himself, in a letter to Paolo Sarpi in 1604.
challenging.for: It seems natural, because a thing that has fallen farther has been pulled for longer.
challenging.against: Galileo later showed it cannot be true, because falling 4 feet and 8 feet would then take the same time. The speed grows with the time of the fall.

challenging.claim: Cats can fall from any height and walk away, because they land on their feet.
challenging.who: A popular belief, partly supported by a study of cats brought to a vet in New York in 1987.
challenging.for: In that study, cats reported to have fallen from higher than about six or seven storeys had fewer injuries on average than cats that fell from fewer. Some scientists think the cats reach their top speed and relax.
challenging.against: Only cats that survive are taken to the vet, so we do not see the ones that did not. A long fall can still kill a cat.

big_questions.q: At top speed, gravity is still pulling a raindrop, yet the raindrop is not speeding up. How can a thing be pulled and not change speed?
big_questions.hint: Think about the push of the air as well as the pull of the Earth.

big_questions.q: A ball moves sideways and falls at the same time, and each movement ignores the other. How can one thing do two separate movements at once?
big_questions.hint: Think about the walking drop, and what the ball was doing before you let go.

big_questions.q: A ball dropped from 4 times higher hits with 4 times as much movement energy. Where did the extra energy come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about the stored energy of a thing held high, and what pulls it down for longer.

big_questions.q: Air pushes back harder as a thing goes faster, until the two forces match exactly. Why does nature find this balance every time, and by itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when the push of the air is a little too small, and when it is a little too big.

big_questions.q: You are moving around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second, and you feel nothing. What else might we be moving along with, without feeling it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the train and the tossed lime.

big_questions.q: A small animal is safe from a fall and a big animal is not. Is being safe a fixed trait, or does it depend on size?
big_questions.hint: Think about the two cubes, and what changed when one became twice as wide.

big_questions.q: Aryabhata's critics had a sensible reason, yet they were wrong. How can a good argument be wrong, and how do we find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about what idea they did not have yet.

big_questions.q: Galileo made a mistake about falling, then found it by thinking. Is thinking enough to find a mistake, or do we need to test as well?
big_questions.hint: Think about how he showed that his first idea could not be true.

story.title: The Lime on the Night Train
story.note: A made-up story. Kavya, Raman Mama and Paati are imagined. The science and history in it are real. Aryabhata did write about a person in a moving boat in the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE. Later astronomers such as Varahamihira and Brahmagupta did argue against a turning Earth, in words much like Raman Mama's. A turning Earth carries a person in Chennai along at about 450 metres every second.
text: Kavya was ten years old, and she was going to Chennai on the night train from Madurai with her uncle. Raman Mama had been a schoolmaster for forty years. He had an opinion about everything, and he liked it best when someone argued with him.

The train clattered through the dark. The lower berth smelled of murukku and of the steel tiffin box that Paati had packed. Raman Mama had an old book open on his knee and his glasses halfway down his nose.

'Listen to this,' he said. 'About fifteen hundred years ago, an astronomer called Aryabhata wrote that the Earth turns round once every day. It is not the stars that move, he said. It only seems so. It is like a man in a boat, who sees the trees on the bank slide backward.'
'That sounds right to me,' said Kavya.

'It sounded wrong to a great many clever people,' said Raman Mama. 'Varahamihira was one. Brahmagupta was another. They asked a simple question. If the Earth turns, and the ground slides away to the east, why is a stone thrown straight up not left behind? Why does it not fall far to the west? And why does a bird that leaves her nest ever find the nest again? Answer that, Kavya, and I will believe you.'
Kavya thought hard. She did not know. Her mother always said that a girl who does not know should say so, and then go and find out.
'I don't know yet,' she said. 'But I think I can find out right now.'

She reached into Paati's bag and took out a lime. Paati had packed it for the long ride, in case anyone felt sick. Kavya stood in the narrow aisle between the berths, holding the bunk rail with one hand. The train swayed.

'We are going about eighty kilometres an hour,' she said. 'The ground outside is sliding backward, like Aryabhata's trees. If your argument is right, Mama, then a thing thrown up gets left behind. The lime should fly to the back of the carriage.'
She tossed the lime straight up, just above her head.

It rose. It stopped. It fell. It landed in her palm with a tiny slap, in exactly the place where she was standing. She tossed it again, and again. Each time the train rushed forward through the dark, and each time the lime came back to her hand.
'Hm,' said Raman Mama. 'The air in this carriage is moving with us. The roof is over us. That is cheating.'

'Then it is cheating for the bird as well,' said Kavya. 'The air goes round with the Earth, right up high. And the tree, and the nest, and the bird were all going round before she ever left. Look. The lime was already going forward at eighty before I threw it. My throw only added an up. Nothing took the forward away.'

She tossed it once more to show him. 'Up and down is one movement. Forward is another. The Earth pulls only on the up and down. It does not touch the forward. So when the lime comes down, the train has gone forward, and so has the lime, and so have I. We all went the same distance. That is why I am still under it.'
Raman Mama said nothing for a long time. The wheels sang on the rails. Then he took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes.
'Varahamihira asked a very good question,' he said slowly. 'And he did not have a lime.'
'He did not have a train,' said Kavya.

Raman Mama began to laugh, and he laughed until the man in the next berth turned over in his sleep. 'Forty years,' he said. 'Forty years I have taught that argument as a puzzle with no answer. And a girl answered it in the aisle of a train, with a lime from her grandmother's bag.'
'Tell your old class it was Paati's lime,' said Kavya. She sat down on the berth, because the grown-ups had said never to stand for long when the train was moving, and she held the lime in her lap.

At dawn, the train slowed beside a grey sea. A platform slid past the window, with chai sellers and a crow on a pillar. Kavya looked out. The whole of Chennai was being carried round by the Earth at about four hundred and fifty metres every second. Nothing in her cup of tea shook. Nothing in her felt it at all.
She squeezed the lime, and smelled it, and smiled.
story.epiphany: A thing that is moving keeps its sideways speed while it falls. So a tossed lime comes back to your hand, even on a moving train, and a bird can fly back to her nest on a turning Earth.

The lime caught in the girl's open palm, with a faint dotted line showing it moving forward with the train.

roots.context: We have dropped cups and dough and learned how falling things speed up. Now we ask what a lime tossed on a train tells us about being still and being in motion.

deep_truth.truth: When you toss a lime up on a moving train, it falls back into your hand. The lime keeps the train's sideways speed all the way. So being at rest does not mean having no speed. It means moving along together with everything around you.
deep_truth.habit: We call a thing 'still' or 'moving' as if that were a fact about the thing alone. But still always means still compared with something. Seen from the Sun, the room you sit in is moving at about 30 kilometres every second.
deep_truth.evidence: In Toss on the Move, the ball went up and came down into the walker's hand while the walker kept moving. In the Walking Drop, the dough ball landed ahead of the drop mark by about the walking speed times half a second.

three.who_am_i: You are moving right now. You travel around the Earth's axis at hundreds of metres a second and around the Sun at about 30 kilometres a second, and you feel nothing.
three.what_is_life: A falcon folds her wings and dives at more than 200 kilometres an hour. A seed spins down slowly. Each living body meets the same pull and the same air in its own way.
three.what_is_this_world: Dropping, throwing, tossing and walking all follow one rule. Gravity pulls down, and the sideways speed carries on.

roots.thread: Every falling thing near the Earth feels the same pull. A stone, a raindrop, a seed and a mouse all gain speed at the same rate to begin with. The many different kinds of fall come from what the pull meets: the air, the shape, the size and the sideways speed. The air itself is made of the same kind of particles as our bodies. So the fall of a raindrop is a meeting between the Earth, the air and the drop, and none of them is the whole story.

teachings.teaching: A person in a boat moving forward sees still things on the bank moving backward. In the same way, the still stars seem to move west to people on the Earth.
teachings.link: Aryabhata saw that a still thing and a moving thing depend on where you stand. The tossed lime shows the same idea inside a train.

teachings.teaching: It moves, and it does not move. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
teachings.link: In the train, the lime is moving at 80 kilometres an hour and is also at rest in your hand. Both are true, depending on what you compare it with.

science.text: Galileo wrote in 1632 that nothing you do in a smoothly moving ship's cabin shows whether the ship is moving. Physicists call this the relativity of motion. It is settled science.

Measurements of the glow left over from the early universe show that our Solar System moves at about 370 kilometres a second compared with that glow. Whether this counts as a true rest, or only as a handy way to measure, is still debated.

other_view.view: Newton thought that there is a true, fixed space and a true rest, even though we can never find it by experiments inside a ship or a train. He argued that spinning, which we can feel, shows a real kind of motion. Many physicists since have disagreed with him, and say that all motion is measured against something else.

practice.title: Still, and moving
practice.say: Sit very still, with your eyes closed. Feel your feet on the floor and your breath in your belly. Notice that nothing in you feels like it is moving. Now remember that you are being carried around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. Breathe in slowly three times, and notice how quiet that fast movement feels.
practice.kid: Sit very still and close your eyes. Feel your feet on the floor. Breathe in slowly three times. You are moving very fast with everything around you. Can you feel it?

ask: If nothing in a smooth ride shows that you are moving, what does it mean to say that you are still?
Is there anything in the universe that is truly at rest, or is rest always rest compared with something?
You feel a bump when a train brakes or turns, but not when it moves at a steady speed. What is the difference?
roots.art: A girl sitting very still with her eyes closed, while around her faint lines show the Earth turning and the Earth travelling round the Sun.

games.title: Fall Report: what happens to the falling thing?
games.context: This is a question-and-answer game. Each card describes something falling or moving. You say what happens, and then say why.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table with a pencil and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Shuffle them into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading the front of a card aloud while the other players write an answer on small pieces of paper.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a front. The others write an answer.

setup.art: The reader turning the card over to show the answer and the reason, and players holding up their papers.
setup.caption: 3. The reader turns the card over. Everyone checks.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a falling or moving question on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A ball is dropped on a planet with no air. About how fast is it moving after 2 seconds?
items.b: About 20 metres a second. It gains about 10 metres a second every second.

items.f: The same ball keeps falling. About how fast is it moving after 3 seconds?
items.b: About 30 metres a second, which is about 108 kilometres an hour.

items.f: A big raindrop has fallen for 10 seconds from a high cloud. Is it still speeding up?
items.b: No. The push of the air now equals the pull of the Earth, so it falls at a steady speed of about 30 kilometres an hour.

items.f: A skydiver pulls in her arms and legs and dives head first. Does her top speed go up or down?
items.b: Up. She meets less air, so she must fall faster before the push of the air matches her weight.

items.f: A solid rubber ball and a hollow plastic ball are the same size. They are dropped together from a tall tower. Which lands first?
items.b: The rubber ball. It is heavier, so it has a higher top speed in air.

items.f: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the airless Moon. Which lands first?
items.b: They land together. With no air there is no top speed, and everything gains speed at the same rate.

items.f: Meenakshi walks and lets go of a ball above a mark on the floor. Where does the ball land?
items.b: Ahead of the mark. The ball keeps her sideways speed while it falls.

items.f: A ball rolls off a table at the same moment as a ball is dropped from the table's edge. Which hits the floor first?
items.b: Neither. They land at the same moment. Sideways speed does not change how fast a thing falls.

items.f: Farhan tosses an orange straight up inside a smoothly moving train. Does it land in front of him, behind him or in his hands?
items.b: In his hands. The orange shares the sideways speed of the train.

items.f: A car going 30 kilometres an hour needs 5 metres to stop. About how many metres does it need at 60 kilometres an hour?
items.b: About 20 metres. Twice the speed needs 4 times the distance.

items.f: A marble is dropped from 4 times the height. How many times the speed does it hit with, if the air is not in the way?
items.b: Twice the speed. Four times the height gives twice the speed.

items.f: The same marble hits with twice the speed. How many times the movement energy does it have?
items.b: Four times. Movement energy grows with speed times speed.

items.f: A mouse falls down a deep, dry pit. Why is she more likely to survive than a horse?
items.b: She has little weight for the area of her body that the air pushes on, so her top speed is low.

items.f: A cube is made twice as wide. How many times more weight does it have?
items.b: 8 times. 2 times 2 times 2 is 8.

items.f: The same cube is made twice as wide. How many times bigger is its outside area?
items.b: 4 times. 2 times 2 is 4.

items.f: A shooting star glows high in the sky. What heats the air around it?
items.b: Its great speed squeezes the air in front of it, and the squeezed air gets very hot.

items.f: A hammer falls on the Moon. Does it gain speed as fast as on Earth?
items.b: No. It gains speed about six times more slowly, about 1.6 metres a second every second.

items.f: Galileo first thought that the speed of a falling thing grows with the distance it has fallen. What did he find out later?
items.b: The speed grows with the time of the fall.

items.f: A washer on a string and three washers on a string of the same length are swinging. Which swings faster?
items.b: Neither. They swing at the same rate. The length of the string decides.

items.f: A raindrop falls 2 kilometres and does not hurt. Why not?
items.b: The push of the air grows with speed until it equals the pull of the Earth, so the raindrop falls at about 30 kilometres an hour.

printables.title: A score sheet with a column for each player
items: Player name, then one box for every card

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player writes an answer on a small piece of paper. They write what happens and one reason.
The reader reads the back. A player scores one point for the right answer. A player scores one more point for a good reason.
The reader decides about the reason, using the back of the card. A reason that says the same thing as the back is good.
After each card, the job of reader passes to the player on the left.
With two players, the parent and the child swap the reader's job after every card.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile. Give each player a pencil and some small pieces of paper.
flow.say: These cards ask what happens when things fall or move. We write an answer and a reason. Then we check the back.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Take a pencil and some paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fall Report. You set up the cards and the paper.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, the reader reads the back aloud. Keep a tally of points on the score sheet.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone writes an answer and a reason. Now the reader reads the back. Who gets a point?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Write your answer and a reason. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the cards about speeding up have in common?
good: Falling things gain the same speed each second.
The air only matters at higher speeds.
The numbers go up by 10 each time.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep the tally going.
flow.say: Keep going. Think about the push of the air. Think about sideways speed. Think about weight and size.
flow.kid: Play on. Think about air, sideways speed, and weight.

ask.q: Which card surprised you so far, and why?
good: The ball landing ahead of the mark.
The mouse surviving the fall.
The orange landing in the hand.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about what made the answer in each case: the pull, the air, the sideways speed or the size.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask each player which card was the hardest, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was hardest? What would help you answer it next time?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Which card would have a different answer on the Moon?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fall Report. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Liner Stacks: does a heavier stack fall faster in air?
experiments.question: Four paper cupcake liners fit inside each other as one stack. Does a stack of four liners fall faster than one single liner, or do they land together?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the stack of four land first, last or together with the single liner? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every liner is the same. Every drop starts from the same height, marked with tape on the wall. Every liner is held with its opening facing up and is let go, not thrown. Only the number of liners changes. Each stack is dropped three times, because one drop can be a fluke, and a drop where the liner tumbles over is repeated. A phone stopwatch started by hand is off by about 0.2 to 0.3 seconds, so only a gap bigger than that is real.

materials.item: 5 paper cupcake or muffin liners, all exactly the same (the bigger and lighter, the clearer the result), or 5 shallow cones cut from newspaper (see step 2)
masking tape
a phone with a stopwatch
a grown-up who can reach about 2 metres up, and a helper to time (with 2 to 4 children, one child times, one watches from the side, one writes; swap after each stack)
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: The grown-up drops the liners while standing on the floor. Nobody stands on a chair or a stool. Keep the small liners away from very young children, who might put them in their mouths. A grown-up does any cutting with scissors if you make newspaper cones. Keep the area under the drop clear of toys and wet floor.
experiments.record: For each stack, write the three times and the middle time. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each stack, using the middle time.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you drop one cupcake liner and stacks of two, three and four liners. You find out whether a heavier stack of the same shape falls faster in air.

setup.art: Four paper cupcake liners nested into a single liner, a stack of two, a stack of three and a stack of four, standing in a row on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Make stacks of one, two, three and four liners.

setup.art: A strip of masking tape on a wall at the height of a grown-up's raised hand, with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the drop height on the wall.

setup.art: A grown-up holding one liner in the left hand and a stack of four in the right hand, both at the tape mark with their openings facing up.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a single liner and a stack of four at the mark, and let go together.

setup.art: A child crouching at floor level with a phone stopwatch while a liner floats down past the tape mark.
setup.caption: 4. Time each fall from letting go to touching the floor.

setup.art: A bar chart on paper with four bars for the stacks of one, two, three and four liners, the tallest for one liner.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each stack.

flow.do: Show your child one liner and a stack of four. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both at the top of the results table.
flow.say: I will drop one liner and a stack of four liners. Which will land first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One liner or a stack of four? Which lands first? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will land first?
good: The stack is heavier.
They are the same shape, so they land together.
The air will hold up the single one.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say they will land together, because heavy and light things fall together. That is a good reason to test it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Liner Stacks test. You guess before you drop anything.

flow.do: Check that all five liners are exactly alike. Stick a strip of tape on the wall at the height of the grown-up's raised hand. Always drop from this height. No liners? Cut five circles from newspaper, 12 centimetres wide, using a katori as a guide. Cut a slit to the middle of each and overlap the cut edges by 1 centimetre. Tape them into five shallow cones.
flow.say: All the liners must be the same. The drop height must be the same too. We will mark it on the wall.
flow.kid: Check the four liners are the same. Put tape on the wall to mark the drop height.
flow.parent: The grown-up should do every drop, holding the liners at the tape with a straight arm. A child on tiptoe changes the height each time. Press nested liners together so they act as one thing.

check.q: Why do we mark the drop height on the wall?
options: So every drop starts from the same height
So the liners fall more slowly
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the drops started from different heights, we would not know whether the number of liners or the height changed the time.

flow.context: In this step, you check the liners and mark the drop height.

flow.do: Hold one liner in the left hand and a stack of four in the right hand. Hold both at the tape mark, with the openings facing up. Let go of both at the same moment. A helper watches from the side and says which landed first. Do this three times.
flow.say: Ready, steady, go. Let go of both together. Which one landed first? By a lot or by a little?
flow.kid: Hold one liner and a stack of four at the mark. Let go together. Which lands first?

ask.q: Did the same one land first every time?
good: Yes, the stack landed first each time.
Yes, and the single liner wobbled more.
Mostly, but one drop was a wobble.

flow.parent: A liner that tumbles over is a wobble. Call it a wobble and repeat that drop. The stack of four should land first by a clear gap. If the single liner wins, check that the stack is pressed together and that the openings face up. If they land together, your liners are small and stiff: use a stack of eight against a single one, or use bigger liners or newspaper cones. If nothing differs even then, say so honestly: that is a result too, and the air matters less for small, stiff things. With two or more children, each guesses before every race and keeps a tally of who guessed right.

check.q: The stack of four landed first. In the Drop Race, a heavy bottle and a light bottle landed together. What is different with the liners?
options: The liners are wide and light, so the air pushes on them a lot
The stack of four is magic
check.why: A wide, light thing is slowed a lot by the air. The heavier stack has more weight to fight the air, so it falls faster. A bottle is heavy and compact, so the air hardly matters.

flow.context: In this step, you race a single liner against a stack of four.

flow.do: Drop one liner from the mark. The helper starts the phone stopwatch as it is let go and stops it when it touches the floor. Write the time. Do this three times. Then do the same for stacks of two, three and four liners.
flow.say: Start the stopwatch when I let go. Stop it when the liner touches the floor. Write down the time.
flow.kid: Drop the liners. Time each fall. Write the time in the table.
flow.parent: The times are rough, because a stopwatch is started a fraction of a second late. That is why each stack is dropped three times, and we use the middle time. Typically, one liner takes about 1.2 to 2 seconds and a stack of four takes about 0.8 to 1.2 seconds from 2 metres. Yours may differ, and the times for stacks of two and three may sit close together. Trust the side-by-side race in step 3 most, and the middle times second. A wobble does not count.

check.q: Three drops of a stack took 1.6, 1.9 and 1.7 seconds. Which is the middle time?
check.why: Put the times in order: 1.6, 1.7, 1.9. The one in the middle is 1.7. The middle time stops one odd drop from changing the answer.

flow.context: In this step, you time stacks of one, two, three and four liners, three drops each.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each stack, using the middle times. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each stack. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: Would a stack of a hundred liners fall a hundred times faster?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: the air pushes harder the faster a thing falls. A heavier stack must go faster before the push of the air matches its weight. So it has a higher top speed. Four times the weight gives only about twice the top speed. That is why the stack of four falls faster, but not four times faster.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Liner Stacks test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Walking Drop: where does a ball land if you drop it while walking?
experiments.question: If you let go of a ball while you walk, where does it land: behind the spot below your hand, right under it, or ahead of it? Does it matter how fast you walk?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the ball land behind the mark, under it, or ahead of it? Will walking faster change where it lands? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The ball, the drop height and the mark stay the same every time. You let go as your hand passes the mark and you do not throw. Only your walking speed changes. A helper times each walk along the 3 metre line, so each pace has a real speed: slow is about 6 seconds, easy about 3 seconds, brisk about 2 seconds. You do three drops at each pace, because one drop can be a fluke, and the helper marks the first place the ball touches the floor.

materials.item: a ball of soft atta dough or modelling clay, about the size of a lime, which does not bounce
masking tape or chalk, to make a drop mark and a straight line 3 metres long
about 10 sticky notes or small squares of paper (number each one), and a pencil
a tape measure or a ruler
a phone stopwatch to time each walk along the 3 metre line

a clear dry floor at least 5 metres long, in a hall, corridor or on a terrace, and a helper (with 2 to 4 children: one walks, one marks the landing, one measures, one writes; swap walker after each pace, and each walker keeps their own table)
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Walk, never run. Wear shoes on a dry floor. Clear toys and mats from the path. Atta dough has wheat in it: do not use it if anyone has a wheat allergy (use modelling clay), do not eat it, wash hands after, and wipe up crumbs so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Write the distance from the mark to the landing note for each drop. For each pace, write the middle of the three distances.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you drop a ball of dough as you walk past a mark. You find out where it lands, and how that changes when you walk faster.

setup.art: A line of masking tape 3 metres long on a hall floor, with a short cross-strip of tape near the end for the drop mark.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a walking line and a drop mark on the floor.

setup.art: A girl standing still with her hand over the drop mark and a dough ball falling straight down to a sticky note on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the ball while standing still, as a check.

setup.art: The same girl walking along the line and letting go of the ball as her hand passes the mark, with a helper crouching beside the line.
setup.caption: 3. Walk along the line and let go as your hand passes the mark.

setup.art: A sticky note on the floor where the dough ball first touched, and a tape measure running back to the drop mark.
setup.caption: 4. Measure from the mark to the landing note.

flow.do: Show the dough ball and the drop mark. Ask your child to draw three dots on paper. They show where the ball may land: behind, under or ahead of the mark. Ask her to say why.
flow.say: You will walk past the mark and let go of the ball as your hand passes it. Where will it land? Behind the mark, under it or ahead of it? Why?
flow.kid: Walk past the mark and let go. Where will the ball land? Behind, under or ahead? Why?

ask.q: Will walking faster change where the ball lands?
good: Yes, it will land farther ahead.
No, it will always drop straight down.
It will land behind, because the ball is slow.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the ball falls straight down under the hand. Write it down so they can compare later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Walking Drop. You guess before you walk.

flow.do: Stick the drop mark on the floor. Measure the height of your child's shoulder and write it down. Stand still with your hand above the mark and let go of the ball. The helper puts a sticky note where it lands. Measure from the mark to the note.
flow.say: First we stand still. Let go of the ball above the mark. It should land right under your hand. This is our check.
flow.kid: Stand still over the mark. Let go of the ball. Where does it land?

ask.q: Why did we drop the ball while standing still first?
good: To see what happens with no walking.
So we have something to compare with.
To check our measuring works.

flow.parent: Hold the ball at shoulder height, which is about 1 metre for most children of this age. The standing drop should land within a couple of centimetres of the mark. If it does not, check that the hand really is above the mark.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the mark and drop the ball while standing still. This is the check to compare with.

flow.do: Walk along the tape line at a slow pace. Let go of the ball as your hand passes the mark. The helper puts a note at the first place the ball touches. Do this three times. Then do three drops at an easy pace and three at a brisk pace. Do not run.
flow.say: Slow pace first. Let go as your hand passes the mark. Helper, mark the first touch.
flow.kid: Walk past the mark. Let go as your hand passes it. Slow, then easy, then brisk.
flow.parent: Open the hand to let go. Do not throw or flick. Dough does not bounce, so the first touch is easy to see. If one drop lands far from the other two, repeat it. Most odd drops come from letting go too early or too late; a little scatter of 10 centimetres is normal. Time each walk along the 3 metre line and write the seconds next to the pace. Write each landing on its numbered note and leave the notes on the floor until all nine drops are done. If the ball rolls or squashes unclearly, make it firmer or use a clay ball.

check.q: Meera's ball landed 50 centimetres ahead of the mark when she walked at an easy pace. About where will it land if she walks twice as fast?
check.why: The ball keeps her sideways speed while it falls, and the fall takes the same time. Twice the speed means twice the distance travelled forward in that time.

flow.context: In this step, you walk past the mark at three paces and drop the ball each time.

flow.do: Measure each landing from the mark and write it in the table. Find the middle of the three for each pace. Ask your child what pattern she sees.
flow.say: Look at the three middle numbers. What happens to the landing spot when you walk faster?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. What happens when you walk faster?

ask.q: Did the ball ever land behind the mark?
good: No, it always landed ahead.
No, it kept moving forward with me.
Only when I let go too late.

flow.parent: Typically you will see about 20 to 30 centimetres for a slow pace, about 50 for an easy pace and 70 to 90 for a brisk pace. Your numbers will differ with the size of the child and the pace. A child's speed in metres a second is 3 divided by the seconds; the landing distance should be about half of it in metres. What matters is that faster walking gave a longer distance.
flow.context: In this step, you measure where the ball landed and look for a pattern.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then return the dough and tidy the notes.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: If you could walk twice as fast, where would the ball land?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: the ball was moving forward with your hand before you let go. Letting go took away the hold of your hand, but not the forward speed. The fall from shoulder height takes about half a second whatever your pace. So the ball lands about half your walking speed, in metres, ahead of the mark.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Walking Drop. You explain what you found.

experiments.title: Dents in Dough: does a faster hit dig deeper?
experiments.question: A marble is dropped into soft dough from 10, 20 and 40 centimetres. Does a higher drop dig a deeper dent, and by how much: about the same, twice as deep, or four times as deep?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which height will dig the deepest dent? Will the dent from 40 centimetres be about the same as the 10 centimetre dent, 2 times as deep, or 4 times as deep? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The marble, the dough and the way you let go stay the same. Each drop lands on a fresh patch of smooth dough. Only the drop height changes. Each height is tried three times, because one drop can be a fluke. With 2 to 4 children, a different child drops each of the three tries.

materials.item: a heavy glass marble (a big shooter) or a steel ball, about 2 centimetres wide, from a toy or stationery shop
about 5 cups of atta and some water, kneaded into soft dough (enough for a pad about 18 centimetres square and 2.5 centimetres thick)
a tray or thali, at least 20 centimetres by 30 centimetres
a 30 centimetre ruler, 2 toothpicks, masking tape and a spoon (with 2 to 4 children: one drops, one holds the ruler, one measures, one writes; swap each height)
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep the marble away from children under five, who might put it in their mouths. Atta dough has wheat in it: do not use it if anyone has a wheat allergy (use modelling clay), do not eat it, and wash hands after. Toothpicks are sharp: a grown-up helps, push gently with the point down, and throw them away afterwards. In hot weather, cover the dough with a damp cloth between rounds so it does not dry out.
experiments.record: Write the depth of each dent in millimetres. For each height, write the middle of the three depths. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each height.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you drop a marble into soft dough from three heights. You find out how a faster hit changes the dent.

setup.art: A tray of soft dough pressed flat and smooth, with a spoon smoothing the top.
setup.caption: 1. Press the dough into a thick pad on the tray, about 2.5 centimetres thick. Smooth the top.

setup.art: A ruler standing upright beside the tray, with a marble held by two fingers at the 10 centimetre mark above the dough.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the marble at 10 centimetres above the dough.

setup.art: A marble sitting in a round dent in the dough, with three dents in a row of increasing depth.
setup.caption: 3. Drop it from 10, 20 and 40 centimetres, three times each, on fresh patches 6 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A ruler lying across a dent with a toothpick pushed down to the bottom and pinched at the ruler's edge.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the depth with a toothpick.

flow.do: Show the marble and explain that it will be dropped from 10, 20 and 40 centimetres. Ask your child to guess which dent will be deepest and how much deeper the dent from 40 centimetres will be. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: We drop a marble into soft dough from three heights. Which dent will be deepest? How much deeper will the 40 centimetre dent be than the 20 centimetre dent? Why?
flow.kid: A marble drops into dough from three heights. Which dent is deepest? Why?

ask.q: Will a drop from 4 times the height make a dent 4 times as deep?
good: Yes, 4 times as deep.
No, about twice as deep.
It will be about the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dents in Dough. You guess before you drop the marble.

flow.do: Mix about 5 cups of atta with water until the dough is as soft as an earlobe. Press it into a pad about 18 centimetres square and 2.5 centimetres thick in the tray. Smooth the top with the back of a spoon. Tape a ruler upright beside the tray.
flow.say: The dough must be soft, so the marble leaves a dent. We smooth it flat every time we start.
flow.kid: Make soft dough. Press it flat in the tray. Smooth the top.
flow.parent: If the marble bounces away, the dough is too stiff. Add a spoon of water and knead again. If the marble sinks in completely, add some dry atta. In damp weather the dough turns sticky: knead in dry atta. A good dough gives a dent of about 3 to 10 millimetres from 10 to 40 centimetres; if the 10 centimetre dent is under 2 millimetres, make the dough softer.

check.q: Why do we drop each marble on a fresh, smooth patch of dough?
options: So every drop meets the same kind of surface
So the dents make a nice pattern
check.why: In a fair test only the drop height changes. If a marble landed in an old dent, we would not know whether the height or the old dent changed the result.

flow.context: In this step, you make the soft dough and set up the ruler.

flow.do: Hold the marble with its bottom at the 10 centimetre mark. Let go. Do not push it. Leave the marble in its dent. Do this three times on three fresh patches, about 6 centimetres apart in a 3 by 3 grid. Then do three drops from 20 centimetres and three from 40 centimetres. Do not smooth the dough until all nine dents are measured.
flow.say: Hold the marble at the mark. Let go. Do not push it. Leave it in its dent.
flow.kid: Drop the marble from 10, 20 and 40 centimetres. Do three drops from each height.
flow.parent: Keep the marble from rolling by letting go with a gentle opening of the fingers. Use the whole tray, a new patch each time. If you run out of fresh patches, measure what you have, then smooth the dough flat and carry on.
flow.context: In this step, you drop the marble nine times, from three heights.

flow.do: Lift out each marble. Lay the ruler across the dent. Push a toothpick down to the bottom of the dent. Pinch it at the edge of the ruler, lift it out and measure it. Write the depth in millimetres. Find the middle of the three for each height.
flow.say: Lay the ruler across the dent. Push the toothpick to the bottom. Pinch it at the ruler. Then measure it.
flow.kid: Measure how deep each dent is with a toothpick. Write it down.
flow.parent: The numbers will be small, a few millimetres, so measure carefully. A dent from 40 centimetres is usually clearly deeper than one from 10 centimetres, but dough is soft and springy, so measure to the nearest millimetre and expect a 1 millimetre error. If a dent is hard to read, measure its width across with the ruler too.

check.q: You push a toothpick to the bottom of a dent, with a ruler lying across the top. Where do you pinch the toothpick?
options: At the edge of the ruler
At the tip of the toothpick
At the very top of the toothpick
check.why: The ruler lies at the level of the dough surface. The part of the toothpick below the ruler is the part inside the dent, so pinching at the ruler's edge marks the depth.

flow.context: In this step, you measure how deep each dent is.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each height, using the middle depths. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each height. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: Why does a car going fast need so much more room to stop?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: a marble dropped from 4 times the height lands with twice the speed. In the 1720s, a scientist named Willem 's Gravesande dropped balls into clay, and found that twice the speed made a dent about 4 times as deep. Emilie du Chatelet used this to argue that the strength of a hit grows with speed times speed. Dough is softer and springs back, so in your tray the 40 centimetre dent will probably be about 1.5 to 4 times the 10 centimetre one, not exactly 4. That is normal: real soft things do not follow the neat rule. The sure result is that a faster hit digs deeper. Look for the trend.
flow.context: This is the last step of Dents in Dough. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

activities.title: Toss on the Move: does a tossed ball come back to your hand?

materials.item: a soft ball, a lime, or a pair of rolled-up socks (with 2 to 4 children, take turns; the others watch from the side and call front, behind or in hand)
a clear room or corridor about 5 metres long

schedule.what: Guess. Toss the ball while standing still, then while walking at two paces. Say what you saw.

activities.record: Make a tally for each pace (standing, easy, faster): out of 5 tosses, how many came back to the hand, how many landed in front, how many behind. Compare the three rows.
activities.context: In this activity, you toss a soft ball straight up while you walk. You find out whether it comes back to your hand.

setup.art: A girl standing in a room and tossing a lime straight up above her head, then catching it.
setup.caption: 1. Toss the ball straight up and catch it while standing still.

setup.art: The same girl walking across the room and tossing the lime straight up, with a dotted line showing the lime moving forward with her.
setup.caption: 2. Walk and toss the ball straight up. Catch it.

setup.art: A girl sitting in a train seat tossing a small ball a short way up with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 3. If you travel by train or bus, a grown-up can let you try a very small toss from your seat.

flow.do: Ask your child to toss the ball straight up a little above her head while standing still, and to catch it. Then ask her what will happen if she walks and tosses the ball straight up.
flow.say: You will walk and toss the ball straight up. Will it land in front of you, behind you or in your hand? Why?
flow.kid: Walk and toss the ball straight up. Will it land in front, behind or in your hand? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the ball will land?
good: Behind me, because I moved on.
In my hand.
In front of me, because I am moving.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the ball will be left behind.
flow.context: This is the first step of Toss on the Move. You guess before you try it.

flow.do: Ask your child to walk at an easy pace across the room. She tosses the ball straight up, not forward, a little above her head, and catches it. She does this five times.
flow.say: Walk at an easy pace. Toss the ball straight up. Try to catch it. Do it five times.
flow.kid: Walk. Toss the ball straight up. Catch it. Do this five times.

ask.q: Did the ball ever land behind you?
good: No, it came back to my hand.
No, it moved forward with me.
Once, but I tossed it backward.

flow.parent: Count only good tosses. She must toss straight up, not forward. If the ball goes forward, call it a bad toss and repeat it.
flow.context: In this step, you walk and toss the ball straight up.

flow.do: Ask your child to walk a little faster and do five more tosses. If you are travelling by train or bus today, a grown-up sits next to her. On a smooth, straight stretch, she tosses a soft ball only 20 centimetres up from her seat.
flow.say: Walk a little faster this time. Toss and catch five times. Does the ball still come back to your hand?
flow.kid: Walk faster. Toss and catch five times. Does the ball still come back?
flow.parent: Never stand up in a moving vehicle for this. A seated toss is enough. The ball may drift if the vehicle sways, brakes or turns. That is part of what you are finding out.
flow.context: In this step, you try a faster pace, and you may try a seated toss on a train or bus.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: What would happen to the ball if the train suddenly braked while it was in the air?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: the ball already moved forward with you before you tossed it. Gravity pulls it down but does not take the forward speed away. If the train braked while the ball was up, the ball would keep its old forward speed and land a little ahead of your hand.
flow.context: This is the last step of Toss on the Move. You explain what you found.

activities.title: Cube Animals: a mouse, a cat and a horse made of cubes

materials.item: 27 identical cubes: sugar cubes, dice, wooden or plastic building blocks, or cubes cut from stiff dough
paper and a pencil (with 2 to 4 children, each builds one animal and counts the animal's weight and faces, and the group fills one table)

schedule.what: Build the three cubes. Count the weight and the outside faces of each. Compare.

activities.record: A table with three rows, mouse, cat and horse. In each row write the number of cubes (the weight), the number of outside faces, and the weight for each outside face.
activities.context: In this activity, you build three cube animals of different sizes. You count their weight and the area of their outside to see why big animals fall harder than small ones.

setup.art: A single sugar cube, a 2 by 2 by 2 cube of eight sugar cubes and a 3 by 3 by 3 cube of twenty-seven cubes in a row, labelled mouse, cat and horse.
setup.caption: 1. Build the mouse, the cat and the horse from cubes.

setup.art: A finger pointing at the outside faces of the 2 by 2 by 2 cube, with one face on each side marked with a dot.
setup.caption: 2. Count the faces on the outside of each cube.

setup.art: A table on paper with three rows, cubes, outside faces and weight for each outside face.
setup.caption: 3. Write the numbers in a table.

flow.do: Set one cube on the table. This is the mouse. Count its weight, which is 1 cube. Count the faces on the outside, which is 6. Write both numbers.
flow.say: This one cube is a mouse. Its weight is 1 cube. How many faces are on the outside? Count them.
flow.kid: One cube is the mouse. Count its outside faces. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: The word weight here means the number of cubes. A cube has 6 faces, all on the outside. Before counting, ask for a guess: if the cat has 8 times the weight, will she have 8 times the outside? Dice and small cubes are small parts: keep them from children under five, and do not eat cubes that have been played with.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cube Animals. You count the weight and the outside of the mouse.

flow.do: Build a cube that is 2 cubes wide, 2 deep and 2 high from 8 cubes. This is the cat. The cat weighs 8 cubes. Count the faces on the outside. Each side of the big cube shows 4 faces, and it has 6 sides.
flow.say: The cat is twice as wide, twice as deep and twice as high. Count its weight in cubes. Then count the faces on the outside.
flow.kid: Build the cat from 8 cubes. Count the weight. Count the outside faces.

ask.q: How many times more weight does the cat have than the mouse?
good: 8 times.
8 cubes instead of 1.

check.q: The cat cube has 8 times the weight of the mouse cube. How many times more outside faces does it have?
options: 4 times, which is 24 faces instead of 6
check.why: Each side of the cat shows 2 times 2, which is 4 faces. Six sides make 24 faces. Compared with the mouse's 6, that is 4 times as many. The weight grew 8 times, but the outside grew only 4 times.

flow.context: In this step, you build the cat and count the weight and outside faces.

flow.do: Build a cube that is 3 cubes wide, 3 deep and 3 high from 27 cubes. This is the horse. Count its weight, which is 27 cubes. Count the faces on the outside. Each side shows 9 faces, and it has 6 sides.
flow.say: The horse is three cubes wide, deep and high. Its weight is 27 cubes. How many faces are on the outside?
flow.kid: Build the horse from 27 cubes. Count its weight. Count its outside faces.
flow.parent: The horse has 54 faces on the outside. Check your child's count, because it is easy to miss the bottom.
flow.context: In this step, you build the horse and count its weight and outside faces.

flow.do: Write the weight for each outside face for all three animals. Divide the weight by the number of faces. Ask your child what pattern she sees.
flow.say: Divide each weight by its number of faces. Which animal has the most weight for each bit of outside? What does that tell us about falling?
flow.kid: Divide the weight by the faces. Which cube has the most weight for each outside face?
flow.think: Which animal would have to fall fastest before the air pushed back enough?
flow.parent: The numbers are about 0.17 for the mouse, 0.33 for the cat and 0.5 for the horse. The air can only push on the outside. A bigger animal has more weight for every bit of outside, so she must fall faster before the push of the air equals her weight. That is why her top speed is higher. Stretch: the numbers are the width divided by 6, so a cube 10 wide, an elephant, would have 1000 weight, 600 faces, and 1.67 each.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cube Animals. You compare the three animals.

activities.title: Swings: does a heavy swing swing faster?

materials.item: about 1.2 metres of thin string or strong thread
3 washers or steel nuts, all the same (from a hardware shop for a few rupees), or 1, 2 and 3 five-rupee coins taped together
masking tape, and a table edge or a door frame to hang the string from
a phone with a stopwatch, and a ruler (with 2 to 4 children: one swings, one counts out loud, one times 20 seconds, one writes; swap each try)

schedule.what: Guess. Swing one washer, then three. Then change the string length and count the swings.

activities.record: A table with the string length, the number of washers, and the number of swings in 20 seconds.
activities.context: In this activity, you hang a washer from a string and count its swings. You find out whether a heavier swing is faster, and what does change the swing.

setup.art: A string hanging from a door frame with a single steel washer tied at the bottom, and a ruler measuring 50 centimetres of string.
setup.caption: 1. Hang one washer from a string 50 centimetres long.

setup.art: A child pulling the washer a hand's width to one side and letting go, with a phone stopwatch beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Pull it a hand's width to the side and let go. Count the swings in 20 seconds.

setup.art: Three washers tied to the same string, swinging, beside a string of half the length.
setup.caption: 3. Try three washers. Then try a shorter and a longer string.

flow.do: Tie one washer to the end of the string. Tape the other end so that the string is 50 centimetres long from the tape to the washer. Ask your child to guess whether three washers will swing faster than one. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: A swing is a washer that goes out and back. Will three washers swing faster than one? Will a shorter string swing faster? Why?
flow.kid: Will three washers swing faster than one? Will a short string swing faster? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will change the swing: the weight or the length?
good: The weight, because heavy things are stronger.
The length, because a shorter swing has less distance.
Neither, they will all be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A swing is out and back to where you let go. Keep the swing small, no more than a hand's width from the middle. Keep faces out of the swing path, and keep washers away from very young children.
flow.context: This is the first step of Swings. You build the swing and guess.
