flow.do: Pull the washer a hand's width to one side and let go. Do not push it. Count the swings for 20 seconds with the phone stopwatch. Write the number. Then tie on two more washers and count again.
flow.say: Pull it to the side and let go. Count each swing out and back. Stop at 20 seconds.
flow.kid: Let the washer swing. Count the swings for 20 seconds. Write the number.
flow.parent: Length means from the tape to the middle of the washers. Tie extra washers close together so the middle stays at the same length. For a string 50 centimetres long, typically you will count about 14 swings in 20 seconds. Three washers give the same number, give or take one. A lost count of one or two is normal, so repeat if you are unsure.

check.q: One washer made 14 swings in 20 seconds, and three washers made 14 swings. What does this show?
options: The weight of the swing did not change how fast it swings
check.why: The heavier swing swung at the same rate. The Earth pulls the heavier swing harder, but it is also harder to get moving, and the two cancel, as they do in a fall.

flow.context: In this step, you count the swings of one washer and of three washers.

flow.do: Go back to one washer. Make the string 25 centimetres long and count the swings in 20 seconds. Then make it 100 centimetres long and count again. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Now we change the length. A short string first, then a long one. Count the swings in 20 seconds.
flow.kid: Try a short string and a long string. Count the swings in 20 seconds.
flow.parent: Typically you will count about 20 swings for 25 centimetres, 14 for 50 and 10 for 100. Four times the length gives half the swings. If you get something close, that is the pattern.
flow.context: In this step, you change the length of the string and count again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: Why does a playground swing take longer to swing back and forth when the chains are longer?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: a swing is a fall that keeps turning. Heavy and light things fall at the same rate, and they swing at the same rate too. The length of the string decides the swing. A story says Galileo, aged 19, watched a lamp swing in the cathedral at Pisa and timed it with his pulse. His student Viviani told the story, and historians doubt some of its details.
flow.context: This is the last step of Swings. You explain what you found.

projects.title: Falling on Video: find how fast a ball speeds up

materials.item: a phone that can film video, and a stack of books to hold it still
a bright ball that stands out from the wall, such as a tennis ball or a lime
a tape measure of 2 metres (or a tailor's tape of 1.5 metres, or a ruler and masking tape marked every 20 centimetres)
masking tape for marking the wall
a plain wall, well lit
a phone gallery that can step through a video one frame at a time, or the free VLC player on a computer
a calculator

projects.safety: The grown-up holds and drops the ball while standing on the floor, from a mark they can reach. Nobody climbs on a chair or a stool. Keep the floor under the drop clear, and pick up the ball at once so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Mark the wall. Film three drops. Step through the frames and read the positions. Work out how fast the ball speeds up.

projects.record: A table with the frame number, the time in seconds, the distance fallen in centimetres, and your answer for how much speed the ball gains each second.
projects.context: In this project, you film a ball falling past a measuring tape. You step through the video frame by frame to find how far it falls each moment, and work out how fast it speeds up.

setup.art: A tape measure fixed upright on a plain wall from the floor to 2 metres, with small flags of masking tape every 20 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Fix a measuring tape on the wall and mark every 20 centimetres.

setup.art: A phone on a stack of books two metres from the wall, pointing at the tape.
setup.caption: 2. Put the phone on books, 2 metres from the wall, pointing at the tape.

setup.art: A grown-up standing on the floor, holding a bright ball against the wall at the top mark, with the phone recording.
setup.caption: 3. Press record. Let go of the ball at the top mark.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a video paused with a ball beside the tape at a low mark, with a frame counter below.
setup.caption: 4. Step through the video and read where the ball is.

flow.do: Fix the tape measure upright on a plain wall with tape, from the floor to its top. Stick a small flag of tape every 20 centimetres. Stand the phone on books 2 metres from the wall. Put it at the height of the 1 metre mark, pointing straight at the tape.
flow.say: The tape measure lets us read where the ball is. The flags make it easy to see. The phone must point straight at the wall and stay still.
flow.kid: Fix the tape on the wall. Put tape flags every 20 centimetres. Put the phone on books.
flow.parent: The top mark should be a height the grown-up can reach with a straight arm, about 1.8 to 2 metres. With 2 to 4 children: one drops, one runs the phone, one reads frames, one writes and uses the calculator; swap for the next clip. Stand the phone upright (portrait) so the whole tape fits in the picture. If you only have a 1.5 metre tape, use a top mark at 1.5 metres and use frames 5, 10, 15 only. A plain wall behind the ball makes it easier to see in the video.
flow.context: This is the first step of Falling on Video. You mark the wall and place the phone.

flow.do: Press record on the phone. The grown-up holds the ball against the wall at the top mark and lets go, so that it falls beside the tape. Stop recording. Do this three times and keep the clearest clip.
flow.say: Press record. Hold the ball at the top mark. Let go, with no push. Stop recording once it lands.
flow.kid: Press record. Let the ball fall beside the tape. Do this three times.
flow.parent: Let go by opening the hand, so the ball does not get a push. If the ball swings sideways, repeat. Most phones film at 30 frames every second. Check your settings, because some film at 60: then use frames 10, 20, 30 and 36 and divide by 60. Drop the ball as close to the wall as you can, so it is the same distance from the camera as the tape. Use a bright room, so the ball is sharp.

check.q: Why does the phone stay on a stack of books and not in someone's hand?
options: So the tape and the wall do not move in the video
check.why: If the phone moves, the tape moves in the video, and we cannot trust where the ball is. A still phone gives a fixed picture to measure against.

flow.context: In this step, you film the ball falling past the tape.

flow.do: Play the clearest clip one frame at a time. Find the frame where the ball first moves, and call it frame 0. Move on to frame 5, frame 10, frame 15 and frame 18. At each frame, read where the middle of the ball is on the tape. Write each reading.
flow.say: Find the frame where the ball first moves. Call it frame 0. Then step on five frames and read where the ball is.
flow.kid: Step through the video one frame at a time. Write where the ball is at frame 5, 10, 15 and 18.
flow.parent: Frame 0 is the last frame where the ball is still at the top mark. Being one frame out changes your answer by about 1 metre a second every second, so check a second clip. At 30 frames a second, 5 frames is one sixth of a second. If your phone cannot step one frame at a time, ask a grown-up to load the clip into the free VLC player on a computer. Then press E to move one frame on.
flow.context: In this step, you read where the ball is in several frames.

flow.do: For each frame, work out the time in seconds by dividing the frame number by 30. Work out the distance fallen by taking the reading away from the top mark. Look for a pattern. Then try this for the last frame: change the distance to metres, double it, and divide by the time times the time.
flow.say: Time is the frame number divided by 30. Distance fallen is the top mark take away the reading. What pattern do you see?
flow.kid: Work out the time and the distance for each frame. Look for a pattern.

ask.q: Did the ball fall the same distance in each set of five frames?
good: No, it fell farther each time.
No, the gaps got bigger.
It sped up.

flow.parent: Typically you will see about 14 centimetres at frame 5, 54 at frame 10, 122 at frame 15 and 176 at frame 18, give or take 10 centimetres. The last frame gives 2 times 1.76 metres, divided by (0.6 times 0.6), which is close to 9.8. You are doing well if you get a number between 8 and 12.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the times and distances, and then find how much speed the ball gains each second.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Look at your answer for how much speed the ball gains each second. Is it close to 10 metres a second every second?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: If you filmed a feather in the same way, what would be different?
flow.parent: Listen first. Then say: the ball fell farther in every set of five frames, so it was speeding up. The pull of the Earth is steady, so the speeding up is steady. The number you found is close to 9.8 metres a second every second.
flow.context: This is the last step of Falling on Video. You explain what you found.

challenges.title: Marble to the Cup: hit a hidden target
challenges.problem: A marble rolls down a paper ramp and flies off a table edge. A grown-up puts a cup on the floor, a place you have not seen. You get three tries to land the marble in the cup, and you must choose where on the ramp to let go of it.
constraints: Let the marble go from rest. Do not push it.
The end of the ramp stays at the table's edge.
You may try the ramp only at three marks before the cup is placed.
You get three tries at each cup position.
materials: a marble or a small steel ball
a 30 centimetre plastic ruler with a groove down the middle, or a strip of stiff card from a cereal box folded into a V channel about 30 centimetres long (thin A4 paper works but wobbles)
3 or 4 books to hold the top of the ramp
a table edge and a clear floor
a plastic cup or a katori (a wide one is easier)
masking tape, a pencil, sticky notes, a tape measure and a pinch of flour or atta to dust the landing patch
general: Roll the marble from three marks, 10, 20 and 30 centimetres up the ramp. Measure where it lands each time. Pick the mark whose landing is closest to the cup.
Draw a graph of the release mark against the landing distance, and read the answer for the cup from the graph.
Put a sticky note at each of the three landing spots, and then place the cup between two of them.
creative: Put more marks on the ramp, such as five, so you can aim at more places.
Cut a notch in a ruler to make a gate that lets the marble go from the same spot every time.
Stack two cups, one in front of the other, and aim for the nearer cup first.
challenges.your_turn: Build the ramp and test the three marks. Write down where the marble lands for each. Then ask a grown-up to place the cup. Choose your mark and try. Which mark did you pick, and why?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about sideways speed. You use what you know about falling and sideways movement to hit a target.

setup.art: A folded paper ramp leaning from a stack of books to the edge of a table, with three tape marks along the ramp.
setup.caption: 1. Build the ramp and mark three places on it.

setup.art: A marble leaving the end of a paper ramp at a table edge and landing on a floor, with sticky notes at three landing spots.
setup.caption: 2. Roll from each mark. Put a sticky note where the marble lands.

setup.art: A plastic cup on the floor between two sticky notes and a child choosing a mark on the ramp.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up places the cup. Pick your mark and try to hit it.

flow.do: Make the V channel from the card or the grooved ruler. Lean the top of the channel on a stack of books so the ramp slopes down to the edge of the table. Stick tape across the ramp 10, 20 and 30 centimetres up from the table edge.
flow.say: The marble will roll down the ramp and fly off the table. We mark three places to let it go from. Which mark do you think will send it farthest?
flow.kid: Build the ramp. Put tape marks at 10, 20 and 30 centimetres.
flow.parent: The last 5 centimetres of the ramp should be nearly flat, so the marble leaves in a straight line. With 2 to 4 children: one builds, one lets the marble go, one watches the landing, one measures; the grown-up or another child places the cup. Tape the ramp so it does not move between tries. Pick up marbles from the floor at once, because a marble underfoot can make someone slip, and keep them away from very young children.
flow.context: This is the first step of Marble to the Cup. You build the ramp.

flow.do: Let the marble go from the 10 centimetre mark. Put a sticky note where it first lands. Measure from the table's foot to the note. Do this three times and keep the middle distance. Then do the same for the 20 and 30 centimetre marks.
flow.say: Let the marble go from the first mark. Where does it land? Put a note there. Try it three times.
flow.kid: Let the marble go from each mark. Put a note where it lands. Measure the distance.
flow.parent: Dust a thin patch of the floor with flour where the marble lands: the first touch leaves a dot. Sweep up afterwards, because flour is slippery. Typically the marble lands about 20 to 50 centimetres from the table's foot. Expect the landing to get farther as the mark gets higher, but not twice as far. A marble leaves the table faster from a higher mark. The fall to the floor takes the same time for all of them.
flow.context: In this step, you test the three marks and record where the marble lands.

flow.do: Leave the room, or close your eyes. The grown-up puts the cup on the floor between the nearest and farthest landing spots. Look at the cup. Pick a mark, and let the marble go. You get three tries. Count the hits.
flow.say: Look at the cup. Which mark will you choose? Why? Let the marble go. How close was it?
flow.kid: Look at the cup. Choose a mark. Let the marble go. Count your hits.

ask.q: How did you choose your mark?
good: I picked the mark that landed closest to the cup.
I guessed between two marks.
I used my sticky notes.

flow.parent: A grown-up chooses a cup place that is between two of the landing spots, so the child must work between marks. If the cup is hit, move it and try again.
flow.context: In this step, you aim at the hidden cup and try to hit it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say how she chose her mark. If she missed, try a mark in between the two that she tested. Then ask why the marble took the same time to land from every mark.
flow.say: How did you choose your mark? If you missed, what could you try next? Why did the marble land at different places, but take the same time to fall?
flow.kid: How did you pick your mark? Why did the marble land in different places?
flow.think: What would change if the table were twice as high?
flow.parent: The marble leaves the table at a different sideways speed from each mark. The fall from the table takes the same time, because gravity pulls down in the same way. A faster marble travels farther in that time. A higher table gives a longer fall, so the marble lands farther away.
flow.context: This is the last step of Marble to the Cup. You explain how you chose.

worksheets.title: Falling, Speeding Up and Top Speed (core)

items.p: A ball falls with no air in the way. About how fast is it moving after 2 seconds?
opts: 20 metres a second
10 metres a second
5 metres a second
items.why: A falling thing gains about 10 metres a second every second. After 2 seconds, 2 times 10 is 20 metres a second.

items.p: A falling stone gains about ____ metres a second of speed every second, when the air is not in the way.
items.why: The steady pull of the Earth adds about 10 metres a second to the speed every second. The exact number is 9.8.

items.p: A coconut falls from a palm with no air in the way. How fast is it going after 4 seconds, in metres a second?
items.why: Each second adds 10 metres a second. 4 times 10 is 40.

items.p: A raindrop that falls from a high cloud keeps speeding up until it hits the ground.
items.why: False. The push of the air grows as the drop speeds up. When it equals the pull of the Earth, the drop stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed.

items.p: What is terminal speed?
opts: The top speed of a falling thing in air, when the push of the air equals the pull of gravity
The speed at the end of a railway line
The speed a thing has just after it is dropped
items.why: At terminal speed the push of the air up equals the pull of gravity down. Nothing is left to speed the thing up, so it falls at a steady speed.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the push of the air against a moving thing
the steady top speed of a falling thing in air
how fast the speed of a thing is changing
how fast a thing moves along, not up or down
items.why: Air resistance is the push of the air. Terminal speed is the top speed in air. Acceleration is how fast speed changes. Sideways speed is movement along, not up or down.

items.p: Sort each fall by what happens to its speed.
items: A hammer falling on the Moon for 3 seconds
A raindrop falling from a high cloud
A pebble dropped from a first-floor balcony
A feather falling in a room
A ball falling in a vacuum chamber
items.why: With no air, a fall keeps speeding up. In air, a long fall reaches a top speed. A feather reaches its top speed almost at once. A short fall of 3 metres is too short for the air to matter much.

items.p: A ball thrown hard sideways takes longer to land than a ball dropped from the same height.
items.why: False. Gravity pulls both balls down in the same way. The ball thrown sideways lands farther away, but it lands at the same moment.

items.p: Kavya walks and lets go of a ball above a mark on the floor. Where does the ball land?
opts: Ahead of the mark
Right under her hand, on the mark
Behind the mark
items.why: The ball keeps her sideways speed while it falls, so it moves forward as it drops. It lands ahead of the spot under her hand.

items.p: Put these in the right order to show what happens to a raindrop falling from a cloud.
a: The drop starts at rest and gravity pulls it down
The faster drop meets more air, so the push of the air grows
The push of the air grows until it equals the pull of gravity
The drop falls at a steady speed
items.why: The drop speeds up, so the air pushes back harder. When the push equals the pull, the drop stops speeding up and falls steadily.

items.p: A stack of four liners falls faster than one liner. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: The stack is heavier, so it must go faster before the push of the air matches its weight. So it has a higher top speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the air pushes harder as the speed grows, and that a heavier thing needs more speed before the push equals its weight.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A raindrop at its top speed, a skydiver at her top speed, a parachutist drifting down steadily, a stone in the first second of a drop.
items.a: The stone in the first second, because it is still speeding up. The others fall at a steady speed.
items.why: The first three have reached a steady speed because the air pushes back as hard as the Earth pulls. The stone has only just started to fall.

items.p: Draw a skydiver falling at her top speed. Draw one arrow for her weight and one arrow for the push of the air. Make the arrows the right lengths.
items.a: A skydiver with a downward arrow for weight and an upward arrow for the push of the air, both the same length.
items.why: At top speed the two forces are equal, so the arrows are the same length. A strong drawing shows weight pointing down and the push of the air pointing up.

items.p: Anita says: 'A falling thing keeps speeding up until it lands.' Say when she is right and when she is wrong.
items.a: She is right for a short fall, or when there is no air, as on the Moon. She is wrong for a long fall in air, where the push of the air grows until the thing falls at a steady speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the air makes the difference, and gives an example of each case, such as a dropped pen and a raindrop.

items.p: Why can a mouse survive a fall that would break a horse?
opts: She has little weight for the area of her body that the air pushes on, so her top speed is low
Mice have much stronger bones than horses
Gravity pulls mice less than horses
items.why: A small body has less weight for each bit of outside. The air stops it speeding up at a lower speed, so she lands gently.

worksheets.title: Why Things Fall the Way They Do (stretch)

items.p: Two things have the same shape and size. One is four times heavier. About how do their top speeds in air compare?
opts: The heavier one has about twice the top speed
The two have the same top speed
The heavier one has four times the top speed
items.why: The push of the air grows as speed times speed. To get four times the push, a thing needs only twice the speed. So four times the weight gives about twice the top speed.

items.p: A marble dropped from 10 centimetres makes a dent 3 millimetres deep. Dropping it from 40 centimetres gives it twice the speed. If twice the speed makes a dent 4 times as deep, how deep is the new dent, in millimetres?
items.why: 4 times 3 millimetres is 12 millimetres.

items.p: A car going twice as fast needs twice the distance to stop.
items.why: False. Twice the speed gives four times the movement energy, so the car needs about four times the distance to stop.

items.p: Twice the speed gives ____ times the movement energy.
items.why: Movement energy grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed gives 2 times 2, which is 4.

items.p: A ball is dropped from the height of a table on the Moon and another on Earth. Which lands first, and why?
opts: The one on Earth, because the Earth pulls harder and the ball gains speed faster
The one on the Moon, because the ball is lighter there
They land together, because gravity is the same everywhere
items.why: The Moon pulls about six times less than the Earth, so a ball gains speed about six times more slowly there. It takes about 1.1 seconds, against 0.45 seconds on Earth.

items.p: Match each cube to its weight, counted in small cubes.
items.why: The weight of a cube is its width times its width times its width. 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. 3 times 3 times 3 is 27. 4 times 4 times 4 is 64.

items.p: A cube is made twice as wide. Sort each thing by how many times bigger it becomes.
items: The number of small cubes in it
The number of faces on its outside
The area that the air pushes on
items.why: Weight and the number of small cubes follow width times width times width, so they grow 8 times. The outside follows width times width, so it grows 4 times.

items.p: Rani walks and drops a ball. It lands 40 centimetres ahead of the mark. She walks twice as fast. About how far ahead does it land?
opts: About 80 centimetres
About 40 centimetres
About 20 centimetres
items.why: The fall takes the same time. At twice the sideways speed, the ball travels twice as far forward in that time.

items.p: A ball falls for 0.5 seconds while a girl walks at 2 metres a second. How many metres ahead of the mark does it land?
items.why: Distance ahead is speed times time. 2 metres a second times 0.5 seconds is 1 metre.

items.p: Put these in the right order to show how Galileo showed his first idea about falling was wrong.
a: He thought that speed grows with the distance fallen
Then falling 8 feet would give twice the speed of falling 4 feet
So falling 8 feet would take the same time as falling 4 feet
Equal times for different distances would mean no time at all
So the speed must grow with the time of the fall
items.why: Galileo followed his first idea to the end and found that it gave an impossible result. So the idea had to be wrong.

items.p: A lime is tossed straight up in a smoothly moving train. Explain why it lands back in the thrower's hand.
items.a: The lime already moves forward with the train. Gravity pulls it down but does not take the forward speed away, so it moves forward as far as the thrower does.
items.why: A strong answer says that the lime shares the train's sideways speed and keeps it while it goes up and down.

items.p: Two astronomers argue about whether the Earth turns.

views.who: The first astronomer (an imagined view, like those of Varahamihira and Brahmagupta)
views.says: If the Earth turned, a stone thrown straight up would land far behind the thrower.

views.who: The second astronomer (an imagined view, in the spirit of Aryabhata)
views.says: The stone already shares the Earth's sideways speed, so it comes back to the thrower, like the lime on the train.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What test could you do to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a test, such as tossing a ball up on a moving train or while walking and seeing where it lands.
items.why: The first argument is sensible but misses one idea. A thing in the air keeps the sideways speed it had. The test with a ball tossed on the move shows this.

items.p: Draw the path of a ball rolled off a table and the path of a ball dropped from the table's edge. Show where each is after each tenth of a second.
items.a: Two dotted paths starting at the table's edge. The dropped ball goes straight down. The rolled ball curves out. At each tenth of a second, both are at the same height.
items.why: Both balls fall in the same way, so the dots are at the same height at the same moment. The rolled ball also moves sideways at a steady speed.

items.p: A coin is dropped from a very tall building. Say why it does not hit the ground with the speed of a bullet.
items.a: The coin tumbles and the air pushes back harder as it speeds up. It reaches a top speed of about 50 to 80 kilometres an hour, far slower than a bullet.
items.why: A strong answer says that the push of the air grows with speed until it equals the pull of the Earth, and so the coin stops speeding up.

items.p: Which sentence matches Galileo's later and correct idea about falling?
opts: The speed of a falling thing grows with the time it has fallen
The speed of a falling thing grows with the distance it has fallen
Heavy things always fall faster, even in a vacuum
items.why: In Two New Sciences in 1638, Galileo gave the rule that speed grows with time. Falling things gain the same speed each second.

worksheets.title: Work It Out: Falling in the Real World (challenge)

items.p: A cliff diver falls for 2 seconds with no air in the way. How fast is she going at the end, in kilometres an hour? (10 metres a second is 36 kilometres an hour.)
items.why: After 2 seconds she is going 20 metres a second. 20 is 2 times 10, so the speed is 2 times 36, which is 72 kilometres an hour.

items.p: A steel ball and a wooden ball are the same size. They are dropped together from a high tower. Which lands first in air?
opts: The steel ball, by a little, because it is heavier and has a higher top speed
The wooden ball, because it is lighter
They land together, because all things fall alike
items.why: The air pushes on both balls equally at the same speed. The steel ball is heavier, so it needs a higher speed before the air matches its weight. In air, it lands first.

items.p: You want a parachute to land a heavier load as gently as a lighter one. Say what you would change and why.
items.a: Make the parachute bigger. A bigger area meets more air, so the push of the air matches the heavier weight at a lower speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that more area gives more push from the air, so the top speed is lower even with more weight.

items.p: A raindrop at its top speed is no longer pulled by gravity.
items.why: False. Gravity keeps pulling the drop all the time. At top speed the push of the air is just as big, so the two cancel and the speed stops changing.

items.p: A skydiver opens her parachute at 200 kilometres an hour. Straight after it opens, which is bigger, the push of the air or her weight?
opts: The push of the air, so she slows down
Her weight, so she speeds up
They are equal, so she keeps the same speed
items.why: The open parachute meets far more air. At 200 kilometres an hour, the push is much larger than her weight, so she slows until the two match again at a lower speed.

items.p: Match each world to how long a ball dropped from 1 metre takes to land.
items.why: The stronger the pull, the faster the ball gains speed, and the less time the fall takes. The Moon pulls least and Jupiter pulls most.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A smooth train at a steady speed, a ship at a steady speed, the Earth turning, a bus braking hard.
items.a: The bus braking hard, because you can feel it. Smooth, steady motion cannot be felt from the inside.
items.why: A change in speed pushes your body. Smooth motion at a steady speed does not, so nothing inside the train, the ship or the Earth shows that it is moving.

items.p: A car needs 5 metres to stop from 30 kilometres an hour. Three times the speed needs 3 times 3 times the distance. How many metres does it need from 90 kilometres an hour?
items.why: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 5 metres is 45 metres.

items.p: A ball moving at 5 metres a second has 25 units of movement energy, which is 5 times 5. How many units does it have at 10 metres a second?
items.why: 10 times 10 is 100. The speed doubled, and the movement energy became 4 times as big, since 25 times 4 is 100.

items.p: J. B. S. Haldane wrote that a mouse can fall down a mine shaft and walk away. What is the main reason?
opts: A mouse has little weight for the area the air pushes on
A mouse falls more slowly because gravity is weaker for her
A mouse always lands on her feet
items.why: A small body has a low top speed, so she lands softly. The Earth pulls a mouse in the same way as a horse. The difference is in how much air she meets for her weight.

items.p: Heavy things fall faster, and heavy and light things fall together. Both sound true. Explain when each one is true.
items.a: In a vacuum, heavy and light things fall together. In air, a heavier thing of the same shape and size falls faster, because it has a higher top speed.
items.why: A strong answer separates the two cases by the air, and says that the push of the air is what makes a difference.

items.p: Hira and Dev read that cats survive falls from tall buildings.

views.says: Cats can survive any fall, because they land on their feet and relax.
We only hear about the cats that were brought to the vet. The ones that died are not in the study.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you need to know to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and says what more we would need, such as how many cats fell in all and how many died.
items.why: Both have a point. A study of cats that reached a vet can miss the cats that did not survive. A long fall can still kill a cat.

items.p: Draw dots to show where a ball thrown sideways is after each tenth of a second. Show that it moves the same distance sideways each time, and farther down each time.
items.a: A row of dots in a curve. The dots are the same distance apart across the page and the gaps between them go down more and more.
items.why: The sideways speed stays the same, so the dots are evenly spaced across. The falling speed grows, so the dots drop farther each tenth of a second.

items.p: Put these in order to show what happens to a shooting star.
a: A speck of rock hits the Earth's air at great speed
The air in front of it is squeezed and gets very hot
The heat makes the speck glow
The speck boils away high above the ground
items.why: The great speed squeezes the air in front of the speck. The squeezed air gets hot, and the heat makes the speck glow and boil away.

items.p: Make up a question about falling that nobody has asked you. Say how you could test it with things at home.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer is a question that a test can answer, and a plan that changes only one thing and repeats the test.
items.why: Good scientists ask new questions and plan fair tests. A good question names the thing you change and the thing you measure.

quiz.p: With no air in the way, how much speed does a falling thing gain each second?
opts: About 10 metres a second
About 1 metre a second
About 100 metres a second
quiz.why: Near the Earth, a falling thing gains about 10 metres a second of speed every second. The exact number is 9.8.

quiz.p: Why does a big raindrop stop speeding up?
opts: The push of the air grows until it equals the pull of gravity
Gravity stops pulling at a height of 100 metres
The raindrop runs out of energy
quiz.why: The faster the drop falls, the harder the air pushes back. When the push equals the pull, the speed stops changing. Gravity has not stopped pulling.

quiz.p: A stack of four paper liners falls faster than one liner. What is the best reason?
opts: The heavier stack must go faster before the push of the air matches its weight
Gravity pulls the stack with a different kind of force
The stack of four is bigger
quiz.why: Both have the same shape. The stack is heavier, so it needs a higher speed before the air pushes back as hard as the Earth pulls.

quiz.p: You let go of a ball while walking. Where does it land?
opts: Ahead of the spot under your hand, because it keeps your sideways speed
Behind you, because you moved on
Right under your hand
quiz.why: The ball was moving forward with you before you let go. Gravity pulls it down but does not take the forward speed away.

quiz.p: A dropped marble hits the dough with twice the speed. How much more movement energy does it have?
opts: 4 times as much
2 times as much
8 times as much
quiz.why: Movement energy grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed gives 2 times 2, which is 4 times the energy.

quiz.p: A cube is made twice as wide. What happens to its weight and to its outside area?
opts: Weight grows 8 times and area grows 4 times
Both grow 2 times
Weight grows 4 times and area grows 8 times
quiz.why: Weight follows width times width times width, which is 8 for twice as wide. Area follows width times width, which is 4.

quiz.p: A ball thrown sideways and a ball dropped from the same height reach the ground at the same moment.
quiz.why: True. Gravity pulls both balls down in the same way. The sideways speed changes only how far away the ball lands.

quiz.p: Galileo's first idea was that the speed of a falling thing grows with the distance it has fallen. How did he show it was wrong?
opts: He saw that falling 4 feet and 8 feet would take the same time, which is impossible
He dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa
He measured the speed with a very fast clock
quiz.why: If speed grew with distance, the two falls would take equal times, which would mean no time at all. So the speed must grow with time.

quiz.p: A ball is tossed straight up in a smoothly moving train, and it comes back to the thrower's hand. What does this show?
opts: The ball keeps the train's sideways speed while it goes up and down
The train must be standing still
Gravity does not work in trains
quiz.why: The ball shared the sideways speed of the train before it was tossed, and it kept it. It moved forward as far as the thrower did.

quiz.p: A mouse survives a fall that would hurt a horse. Which fact explains it best?
opts: A smaller animal has less weight for the area of her body that the air pushes on
Mice are always lucky
Mice fall at the speed of a feather
quiz.why: Weight grows faster than outside area as an animal gets bigger. A mouse has a low top speed, and a horse has a high one.

quiz.p: A car going 30 kilometres an hour needs 5 metres to stop. How far does it need at 60 kilometres an hour?
opts: About 20 metres
About 10 metres
About 5 metres
quiz.why: Twice the speed gives four times the movement energy, so about four times the distance. 4 times 5 is 20.

quiz.p: What does a skydiver do to fall faster?
opts: Pulls in her arms and legs and dives head first, to meet less air
Spreads her arms and legs wide
Puts on a bigger coat
quiz.why: A smaller shape meets less air, so the push of the air matches her weight only at a higher speed.

applications: Designing parachutes: a bigger canopy gives more push from the air, so a heavier load lands at a safe speed.
Setting speed limits near schools, because twice the speed means four times the movement energy and about four times the distance to stop.
Catching a ball in cricket: a fielder judges the curved path of the ball, which is a sideways movement and a fall added together.
Heat shields on spacecraft that come back to Earth, which protect against the hot squeezed air in front.
Choosing the right size of a seed or a drone for the job: a larger area for the weight means a slower fall.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a falling leaf or sheet of paper flutter and tumble, and where will it land?
open_questions.why_open: The air swirls around a falling flat thing in very complicated ways. Computers can model it, but scientists cannot yet predict exactly where one leaf will land.

open_questions.q: Does antimatter fall in exactly the same way as ordinary matter?
open_questions.why_open: In 2023, an experiment at CERN saw atoms of antihydrogen fall downward. The measurement is still rough, so scientists are building better tests.

open_questions.q: Can anything be truly at rest?
open_questions.why_open: Motion is always measured against something else. Scientists disagree about whether there is any special rest that all motion could be measured against.

open_questions.q: Why do tests of falling find that everything falls alike, with no exceptions yet?
open_questions.why_open: Tests have shown it to about 1 part in 10 to the power of 15. Einstein explained it with curved space and time, but nobody knows whether a deeper theory will show a tiny difference.

open_questions.q: What is the quickest way an animal can fall without getting hurt?
open_questions.why_open: Cats, flying squirrels, spiders and seeds all do it in different ways. Scientists are still working out how much of the saving comes from shape, from size and from the way the body bends on landing.

ask_kids: What do you think is the fastest speed you can fall at, and what would decide it?
On the way to school, which things do you see moving along with you? Which of them are you moving along with?
Why do you think a stream from a tap gets thinner as it falls?
If you tossed a ball up in a bus, what would you expect? How could you test it safely?
Which would you rather drop from a roof, an ant or a coconut, and why?

jokes.j: What did the raindrop say when it reached top speed?
jokes.a: I cannot go any faster. The air is pushing me back!

jokes.j: Why did the mouse not mind falling off the shelf?
jokes.a: She was light on her feet, and the air hardly noticed.

jokes.j: What did the ball say to the girl who dropped it as she walked?
jokes.a: Thanks for the lift. I will land a little ahead of you!

jokes.j: Why did the marble make such a deep dent from 40 centimetres?
jokes.a: It fell in with a faster crowd.

jokes.j: Why was the skydiver good at maths?
jokes.a: She always found the top speed.

jokes.j: Why did the single liner lose the race against the stack of four?
jokes.a: It was a lightweight in a heavyweight match.

jokes.j: Why did the lime enjoy the train ride?
jokes.a: It could go up and down without losing its place.

jokes.j: Why did Galileo change his mind about falling?
jokes.a: He found out that 4 feet and 8 feet cannot take the same time.

jokes.j: Which falls faster in air, a cricket ball or a table-tennis ball?
jokes.a: The cricket ball. In a vacuum it would be a draw.

maths.problem: A mango falls from a tree for 3 seconds. With no air in the way, it gains 10 metres a second of speed every second. How fast is it going after 3 seconds, in metres a second and in kilometres an hour? (10 metres a second is 36 kilometres an hour.)
maths.answer: 30 metres a second, which is 108 kilometres an hour.
maths.explain: Each second adds 10, so 3 seconds give 3 times 10, which is 30 metres a second. In kilometres an hour it is 3 times 36, which is 108.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lets you jump straight to the speed after any number of seconds, without adding second by second.

maths.problem: A stone falls 5 metres in the first second, 20 metres in the first 2 seconds and 45 metres in the first 3 seconds. How far does it fall in the second second alone, and in the third second alone? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 15 metres in the second second and 25 metres in the third. The distances 5, 15, 25 go up by 10 each time.
maths.explain: 20 take away 5 is 15. 45 take away 20 is 25. The gaps grow by 10 because the speed grows by 10 every second.
maths.why_maths: Finding how much is added each second shows the pattern behind speeding up. Galileo noticed this pattern.

maths.problem: In the Liner Stacks test, a family found a middle time of 1.8 seconds for one liner and 1.0 second for a stack of four. How much sooner did the stack land? Did four times the weight make the liners land in a quarter of the time? How do you know?
maths.answer: 0.8 seconds sooner. No. The single liner took 1.8 times as long, not 4 times.
maths.explain: 1.8 take away 1.0 is 0.8. 1.8 divided by 1.0 is 1.8, which is much less than 4. Four times the weight gives only about twice the top speed, so the stack is faster, but not four times faster.
maths.context: In the Liner Stacks test, you drop one paper liner and stacks of two, three and four liners, and time each fall.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two times shows how much the extra weight helped, and whether the change was as big as the change in weight.

maths.problem: In the Walking Drop, a ball falls for about 0.5 seconds. Aarav walks at 1 metre a second, Meenakshi at 1.5 metres a second and Farhana at 2 metres a second. How far ahead of the mark does each ball land?
maths.explain: The distance ahead is speed times 0.5 seconds. Half of 1 metre is 50 centimetres. Half of 1.5 metres is 75 centimetres. Half of 2 metres is 100 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Walking Drop, you walk past a mark, let go of a dough ball, and measure how far ahead it lands.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the walking pace by the fall time predicts where the ball lands, so you can check your prediction against your measurements.

maths.problem: In the dents test, a marble dropped from 10 centimetres makes a dent 3 millimetres deep. A drop from 40 centimetres is 4 times the height, so the marble hits with twice the speed, and twice the speed makes a dent 4 times as deep. How deep is the dent from 40 centimetres? What would you expect from 90 centimetres, which is 9 times the height and 3 times the speed?
maths.answer: 12 millimetres from 40 centimetres. From 90 centimetres, 3 times the speed gives a dent 9 times as deep, which is 27 millimetres.
maths.explain: 4 times 3 is 12. Three times the speed gives 3 times 3, which is 9 times the dent. 9 times 3 is 27. Real dough will not match exactly, because it springs back a little.
maths.context: In the dents test, you drop a marble into soft dough from 10, 20 and 40 centimetres and measure the dents.
maths.why_maths: Squares let you predict a dent from a speed, because the effect grows with speed times speed.

maths.problem: Zoya builds a cube 4 cubes wide, 4 deep and 4 high. How many cubes does it weigh? Each side shows 4 times 4 faces. How many faces are on the outside? How many cubes of weight are there for each outside face?
maths.answer: 64 cubes of weight and 96 outside faces. That is 64 divided by 96, which is two thirds, about 0.67.
maths.explain: 4 times 4 times 4 is 64. One side has 16 faces and there are 6 sides, so 96. 64 over 96 is 2 over 3, about 0.67, which is more than the horse's 0.5.
maths.context: In Cube Animals, you build cubes of different sizes and count their weight and their outside faces.
maths.why_maths: Counting weight and outside area shows why a bigger animal has more weight to carry for every bit of outside.

maths.problem: A car at 20 kilometres an hour needs 2 metres to stop. Twice the speed needs 4 times the distance. How many metres does it need at 40 kilometres an hour, and at 80 kilometres an hour?
maths.answer: 8 metres at 40 kilometres an hour and 32 metres at 80 kilometres an hour.
maths.explain: At 40 the speed is twice as big, so the distance is 4 times 2, which is 8 metres. At 80 the speed has doubled again, so the distance is 4 times 8, which is 32 metres.
maths.context: In the dents test, you saw that twice the speed makes four times the effect. The same rule decides how far a car needs to stop.
maths.why_maths: Doubling and doubling again shows how fast stopping distances grow, which is why speed limits matter near schools.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1604, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei wrote a letter to his friend Paolo Sarpi. He had found a rule for falling things and he was sure of it. He thought that the speed of a falling thing grows in proportion to the distance it has fallen. Later he saw that this could not be true. If it were, a stone would take the same time to fall the first 4 feet as to fall 8 feet, because after 4 feet it would be going twice as fast as after 2. Equal times for different distances would mean the fall happened in no time at all, and that is impossible. So the speed must grow with the time of the fall. In 1638, in his book Two New Sciences, Galileo gave the right rule and tested it with balls rolling down slopes. Historians think the argument against the first rule is Galileo correcting his own early mistake.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist (1564 to 1642)
how_we_found_out.when: 1604 (the letter to Paolo Sarpi) and 1638 (the book Two New Sciences)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The speed of a falling thing grows in proportion to the distance it has fallen. Galileo showed it wrong by reasoning: it would make falling 4 feet and 8 feet take the same time, which is impossible. The right rule is that speed grows with time.
